title: Micah 6:9–16
context: The LORD’s voice calls to the city, telling it to “Listen to the rod, and he who appointed it,” and charges it with dishonest measures, violence, and lies. The LORD announces that he has struck the city with a grievous wound, so that the people will eat but not be satisfied and sow but not reap, because “the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of Ahab’s house.” Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: injustice in daily trade and the oppression of the poor bring covenant judgment, as the law and the prophets warn (cf. Lev 19:35–36).

verses.text: The LORD’s voice calls to the city— and wisdom fears your name— “Listen to the rod, and he who appointed it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s voice calls to the city.” Arminian readers note the call to “Listen to the rod, and he who appointed it.”

The line “and wisdom fears your name” is difficult, and translations render it in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the difficult line lightly and read the rod as God’s discipline.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the city is called to hear the LORD behind the coming judgment.

verses.text: Are there yet treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and a short ephah that is accursed?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Are there yet treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and a short ephah that is accursed?” Arminian readers note the charge of cheating in trade.

The short ephah is a false measure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s concern for honesty in ordinary business.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that dishonest gain is wickedness before God, however common it may be.

verses.text: Shall I tolerate dishonest scales, and a bag of deceitful weights?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, “Shall I tolerate dishonest scales, and a bag of deceitful weights?” Arminian readers note that the law required honest weights (Lev 19:35–36).

The LORD will not ignore such fraud.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see justice in commerce as part of covenant faithfulness (cf. Prov 11:1).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God cares about how people buy and sell.

verses.text: Her rich men are full of violence, her inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their speech.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her rich men are full of violence, her inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their speech.” Arminian readers note that injustice reaches every level of society.

The rich use violence and the people speak lies.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see corruption spreading through the community.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the opposite of 6:8: violence instead of justice, and deceit instead of mercy.

verses.text: Therefore I also have struck you with a grievous wound. I have made you desolate because of your sins.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore I also have struck you with a grievous wound. I have made you desolate because of your sins.” Arminian readers note that the judgment is linked to their sins.

The LORD names himself as the one who strikes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s just response to persistent injustice.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s discipline is real and deserved, and both read it as a call to return.

verses.text: You shall eat, but not be satisfied. Your hunger will be within you. You will store up, but not save, and that which you save I will give up to the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You shall eat, but not be satisfied. Your hunger will be within you.” Arminian readers note the futility curses that follow.

What is stored up will not be kept.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear echoes of the covenant curses (cf. Lev 26:26).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that gain without righteousness cannot satisfy.

verses.text: You will sow, but won’t reap. You will tread the olives, but won’t anoint yourself with oil; and crush grapes, but won’t drink the wine.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will sow, but won’t reap. You will tread the olives, but won’t anoint yourself with oil.” Arminian readers note that labor will not bring its expected reward.

The curse touches everyday work.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the covenant warnings coming true (cf. Deut 28:38–40).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of futility under judgment, described plainly.

verses.text: For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of Ahab’s house. You walk in their counsels, that I may make you a ruin, and your inhabitants a hissing. You will bear the reproach of my people.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of Ahab’s house.” Arminian readers note that Judah followed the ways of Israel’s worst kings (cf. 1 Kgs 16:25, 30).

Ahab’s seizure of Naboth’s vineyard (1 Kgs 21) may be in view.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Judah adopting the injustice of the northern kingdom.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that walking in such counsels leads to ruin and reproach.
